lesson.title: Guaranteeing Something Always Happens
lesson.summary: The if-else statement pairs a plain if with a required alternative block, guaranteeing that exactly one of the two branches runs no matter what, unlike a bare if which might run nothing at all.
lesson.body:
The if statement on its own has a gap: when its condition is False, nothing happens in its place, execution simply continues past it. The if-else statement closes that gap by attaching a second block, introduced with the else keyword and its own colon, that runs precisely when the if condition is False. Between the two blocks, exactly one always executes, never both, and never neither. That guarantee, that some branch always runs, is the entire reason to reach for if-else instead of two separate, independently evaluated if statements.

Look at this example:

score = 55
if score >= 60:
    print("Pass")
else:
    print("Fail")

Python evaluates score >= 60 first. With score set to 55, that comparison is False, since 55 is less than 60. Because the condition is False, Python skips the if block entirely and instead runs the else block, printing "Fail". If score had been 75 instead, the condition would be True, the if block would run and print "Pass", and the else block would be skipped completely. In both cases, exactly one line of output is produced, never both "Pass" and "Fail" together, and never neither one.

This is a meaningfully different guarantee than writing two separate if statements, such as if score >= 60: print("Pass") followed on its own by a second if score < 60: print("Fail"). That version happens to produce the same result here, but it does so by evaluating two independent conditions, and it is only correct because those two conditions happen to be exact opposites of each other. The if-else version does not depend on you writing the opposite condition correctly a second time, since not (score >= 60) is guaranteed by Python's logic to be exactly the case where the else branch runs, with no room for the two conditions to accidentally overlap or leave a gap.

That guarantee matters more than it might first appear. With two separate if statements, a typo, such as writing score <= 60 instead of score < 60 for the second check, would create a gap where a score of exactly 60 satisfies neither condition and nothing prints at all, or an overlap where two conditions both fire. The else keyword makes that class of bug structurally impossible, because Python itself determines the else branch as everything the if condition did not cover, rather than asking you to spell out the opposite condition by hand and hoping it lines up exactly.

The if-else statement is also the direct ancestor of two other tools covered next. The elif statement extends this same idea to more than two branches by chaining additional conditions between the if and the else. The ternary expression takes the same two-branch, exactly-one-runs logic and compresses it into a single expression, useful when you want to choose between two values rather than choose between two blocks of statements. Both build directly on the guarantee introduced here: given a condition, one specific outcome is chosen, and the other is not, with no ambiguity about what happens in between.
